name: Kiyomizu-dera
label: Kiyomizu-dera
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '奥の院' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '奥ノ院' (way/102164641): middle (26 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/336641107: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kiyomizu-dera' (532 m across).

text.description:
Kiyomizu-dera, the 'Pure Water Monastery', is a Buddhist temple on the wooded slopes of Mount Otowa in eastern Kyoto, and it is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its Main Hall has a wide wooden stage held up on tall timber scaffolding. Seen from across the valley, that stage looks as if it hangs out over the trees. The current Main Hall dates from 1633, when it was rebuilt after a fire in 1629. In the Edo period, people believed that surviving a 13-metre jump from the stage would grant a wish. 234 jumps were recorded, most of them survived, and the practice was banned in 1872.

The classic photo is the stage seen head-on from the Okuno-in Hall, which sits across the ravine to the north of the Main Hall. From there you get the stage and its scaffolding with trees in the foreground and the city or hills behind. If you have time, there are two other good angles. The small vermilion Koyasu Pagoda makes a colourful foreground with the Main Hall complex across the valley. Down by the Otowa Waterfall you can look up at the scaffolding from below. Okuno-in can be busy, so go early and be patient. Look carefully at your frame for people and branches before you press the shutter. Photography is not allowed inside the Main Hall's inner sanctum.
text.geographic_location: Kiyomizu-dera stands on the Higashiyama hillside in eastern Kyoto, on the slopes of Mount Otowa. The temple complex is large, about 530 m across, and includes the Main Hall, the Otowa Waterfall and several smaller shrines.
text.directions_text: Head for the Higashiyama area of eastern Kyoto and make for the temple on the hillside. Once inside the grounds, leave the Main Hall and follow the walking path around the hillside to reach Okuno-in. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole stage, the trees and the view behind. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the timber scaffolding and bring the stage closer. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the pagoda or waterfall views, where you want to include a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 奥の院 (Okuno-in Hall, across the ravine to the north of the Main Hall). The Main Hall's wooden stage seen head-on from across the valley, with trees in the foreground and the city or mountains behind. Across the ravine to the north of the Main Hall. From the balcony you see the Main Hall's wooden stage head-on across the valley, with trees in front and the city or mountains behind. As an alternative, the Koyasu Pagoda gives a small vermilion foreground with the Main Hall complex beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the stage along a lower line, leaving room for the trees in front and the view behind. Keep your phone level so the timber scaffolding looks straight. For a second picture, move to the Koyasu Pagoda and put its red roof in the foreground. At the Otowa Waterfall, point the phone upwards to catch the scaffolding above the streams of water. Check the edges of the frame for other visitors' heads or phones before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stage to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky behind is bright. Take a few quick frames, as the balcony can be crowded. Tripods are restricted on the stage, but you will not need one for daytime phone photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up around 10 a.m. Some guides also suggest the last hour before closing, so check the temple's current opening times on the official site.

text.access_note: Kiyomizu-dera is a working Buddhist temple and Okuno-in lies inside the paid temple grounds, so check the official site before you go for admission, opening times and any restrictions or renovation works.

name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
label: Kinkaku-ji
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/98115917: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kinkaku-ji' (575 m across).

text.description:
Kinkaku-ji, the Temple of the Golden Pavilion, is a Zen Buddhist temple whose official name is Rokuon-ji. The pavilion is its best-known building. Its top two floors are covered in gold leaf, and it stands at the edge of a pond called Kyōko-chi (Mirror Pond), so the gold and its reflection sit together in one frame. That pairing is why it works so well on a phone: the subject is bright and simple, and the water, trees and sky give you an easy background.

The site was a villa bought by the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu in 1397, and it became a temple after his death. The pavilion you see today dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt after a fire in 1950. It is three storeys and about 12.5 metres tall, and each floor has its own architectural style. The pond holds ten small islands, and the whole garden is designed to be walked around, with different views along the way.

The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south-west of the numbered pin. From there the pavilion is a little over 100 metres away. Start with a wide shot that includes the water, then move closer and look for the reflection. Keep the gridlines on to help you hold the horizon level, and check the edges of the frame for other visitors before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: Kinkaku-ji is in Kyoto, where the temple grounds are laid out around the Mirror Pond.
text.directions_text: Travel to Kinkaku-ji (also called Rokuon-ji) in Kyoto. It is about 100 metres to the south-west of the pavilion. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the pavilion across the water. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the gold floors and roof. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the pond and trees as well, and keep the pavilion away from the edges, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. This gives you a view across the pond to the pavilion.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone sideways and place the horizon on a gridline. Let the pond take up the lower third so the reflection is part of the picture. If you can, include a little of the pine branches or shoreline in the foreground to add depth. Take one wide shot and one zoomed-in shot of the top two floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold leaf keeps its detail and does not turn white. Take a second shot with the exposure slightly higher if the trees look too dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, if you can, when the gold usually looks warm and the paths tend to be quieter. On bright days, the reflection in the pond is usually clearer.

text.access_note: Kinkaku-ji is a working Zen temple and a popular tourist attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry details and any visiting rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Mornings are often quieter than the rest of the day at popular temples in Kyoto.
Gold leaf tends to look warm in low morning light.
Bright, still conditions tend to give a clearer reflection in the pond.
Gold surfaces in strong light can lose detail on a phone unless the exposure is lowered.

name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
label: Fushimi Inari
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2656063038: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fushimi Inari Shrine'.

text.description:
Fushimi Inari Taisha is the head shrine of Inari, the kami of rice and agriculture, and it sits at the foot of Mount Inari (233 metres) in Fushimi-ku. It is best known for its torii gates. The shrine is said to have around 10,000, each donated by a Japanese business, and about 800 of them stand in a row along the main path to form the Senbon Torii, which feels like a tunnel. Near the entrance you will find the two-storey tower gate and the main shrine, whose main hall dates from 1499. Foxes, thought of as Inari's messengers, appear all over the grounds, so look out for the fox statues too.

It photographs well because everything has strong shapes and colour: the bright vermilion gates, the dark wooden buildings and the green hillside behind. On a phone, start at the entrance buildings, where you have room to step back and fit the whole tower gate in the frame. Then walk up to the gate tunnel, where the repeating posts draw the eye along the path. Keep your phone steady and take a few shots of each view, because people will often walk through the frame. The paths up the mountain are long, so you can stop at the first stretch of gates and still come away with plenty of pictures.
text.geographic_location: In Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, at the foot of Mount Inari. The shrine buildings stand at the bottom of the hill, and the gate-lined trails climb up behind them.
text.directions_text: From Kyoto Station, take the JR Nara Line to Inari Station, a ride of about five minutes. The shrine is just outside the station. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower gate and shrine buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you reach the tunnel of torii gates, so you capture the full height of the posts and the length of the path. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for fox statues, carved details and the hanging lanterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gate posts up with the vertical lines so the buildings don't lean. Place the gate or the main hall in the centre, with the vermilion colour filling most of the frame. For the torii tunnel, stand in the middle of the path and point down it, so the gates narrow to a single point. Try one portrait-orientation shot to show the height of the gates and one landscape shot to show the length.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the gate to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly. This keeps the red from washing out and stops the shaded gate tunnel from looking flat. In the tunnel, hold the phone still for a moment before pressing the shutter. After dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning usually means fewer people in your shots. Evening is also good because the approach and main hall are lit through the night. Midday is the busiest and brightest time.

text.access_note: The grounds are open 24 hours and there is no entrance fee, but this is a working place of worship, so be respectful and check the official site before you go.

name: Nishiki Market
label: Nishiki Market
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/772134672: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nishiki Market' (385 m across).

text.description:
Nishiki Market is a narrow, cobbled shopping arcade in downtown Kyoto, often called "Kyoto's kitchen". It runs for roughly 400 metres and has about 130 shops selling fruit, vegetables, fish, dried foods, pickles and more. That makes it a good place for lively, colourful phone photos: stacked produce, hand-written signs, steam from grills and shopfronts packed close together on both sides.

The market has a long history. Fish was being sold in the area as early as the year 782, helped by the cold groundwater that kept it fresh. It received official permission to sell fish in 1615. The cobbled floor you will be standing on was laid in 1984, and the arcade roof above you followed in 1993. One shop, Aritsugu, makes hand-crafted knives and dates from 1560.

Because the lane is narrow, the best pictures usually come from looking along it, with the converging lines of the roof and shopfronts drawing the eye down the street. Then step in close for details such as a tray of pickles or a fish stall. Keep your phone ready but your elbows in: it is a working market and the lane can fill up. Pause at the side so you do not block shoppers, and if you want a close-up of someone's stall, a smile and a quick question go a long way.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of downtown Kyoto, on Nishikikōji Street, one block north of Shijō Street and just west of Teramachi Street. The market stretches west from the Teramachi end towards Takakura Street.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for downtown Kyoto and the Shijō Street area and continue on foot. From Shijō Street, walk one block north to Nishikikōji Street; the market's eastern entrance is by Teramachi Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view along the lane. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) if the arcade feels too tight to fit in, and telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for food and signs without leaning over stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look along the lane from here and keep to the side so you do not block people walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the centre of the lane on a vertical line so the roof and shopfronts lead away from you. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or include a few people for a sense of life. Then move closer for a second shot of one stall, with a tidy display filling the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright stall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so white signs and lights are not washed out. Use portrait mode for close-ups of food, and night mode if the arcade looks dim and your phone offers it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, which makes the lane easier to photograph. The covered arcade gives fairly even light at any time, so you are not relying on sunshine.

text.access_note: The market is a public covered shopping street, but each shop sets its own hours and rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nijo Castle
label: Nijo Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/57111281: large area 'Nijō Castle' (724 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Nijō Castle was built as the Kyoto home of the Tokugawa shōguns. Ieyasu ordered its construction in 1601, and it was completed in 1626 under his grandson Iemitsu. It is one of the seventeen Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto that UNESCO has listed as a World Heritage Site. The grounds cover 27.5 hectares, with two rings of walls and wide moats. That layout gives you plenty to photograph: stone walls, water, gates, gardens and long timber buildings.

The star of the site is the Ninomaru Palace. It is made almost entirely of Hinoki cypress and is decorated with gold leaf, carved wood and paintings by artists of the Kanō school. Its six main buildings are National Treasures. The corridors have the famous 'nightingale floors', which chirp underfoot. That is just clamps moving against nails, not an intruder alarm.

For a phone, the moat-and-wall views and the gate approaches work best, because the strong horizontal lines suit a simple, tidy frame. Switch on gridlines to keep walls and rooflines level. Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then a closer one of a carved or painted detail. Bear in mind that the palace interiors may have their own photography rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Nijō Castle is in Kyoto, to the south-west of the Kyoto Imperial Palace. It sits in its own walled and moated grounds.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Kyoto Imperial Palace area, which lies north-east of the castle, and head south-west on foot or by local transport of your choice. The phone icon on the map is about 240 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the walls, moat and gate together. Use the default lens (1x) for most views, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 240 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the stone walls or rooflines with them so they stay straight. Include some moat water or a gate in the foreground for depth. Once you are inside, frame the Ninomaru Palace's long, low roofline in landscape orientation.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of a pale wall or the sky and lower the exposure slider slightly. This keeps the white plaster and gold details from washing out. Hold the phone steady with both hands for sharp detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually gives softer light and fewer people in your frame. Check the official site for current visiting times.

text.access_note: Nijō Castle is a managed heritage site, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.

name: Yasaka Shrine
label: Yasaka Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maidono (舞殿), Yasaka Shrine' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/328903218: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Yasaka Shrine' (252 m across).

text.description:
Yasaka Shrine sits at the eastern end of Shijō-dōri in Gion. Many people know it as Gion-san. The part that works best on a phone is the Maidono, the dance stage in the grounds beside the main hall. In the evening it is hung with lanterns, and they glow against the darkening sky. The lanterns carry the names of the people who sponsor the festivals, so there is plenty of small detail close up as well as the bigger view.

The shrine is old. Building began in 656, and it was once called Gion Shrine. It is dedicated to Susanoo and is tied to the Gion Matsuri, which takes place every July. In April, crowds pass through the grounds on their way to Maruyama Park for the cherry blossom.

For photographs, aim to arrive as the light fades, so you catch the lanterns once they are lit and the sky still has some colour. The area near the entrance gets busy, and early morning is the calmest time if you want fewer people in the frame. If you have a few spare minutes, the vermilion west gate (Nishiromon) is a good second picture, looking up at its tall tower. Please keep to the paths and be considerate of people who have come to pray.
text.geographic_location: Yasaka Shrine is in the Gion district of Kyoto, at the east end of Shijō-dōri. Maruyama Park is nearby.
text.directions_text: Start from the Gion district and head east along Shijō-dōri to its end, where the shrine stands. If you are coming from elsewhere in Kyoto, get to the Gion district and walk from there. Once inside the grounds, follow the main path to the dance stage beside the main hall. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole stage with its rows of lanterns. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lantern details and names.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the lantern-hung stage packed with hanging lanterns, glowing against the evening sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the stage level, so the rows of lanterns look tidy. Fill the top of the frame with lanterns and leave a strip of evening sky above them. For a different picture, the vermilion Nishiromon Gate (西楼門) is worth a look, shot from below with its tall tower rising above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lantern to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights don't turn into white blobs. As it gets darker, let night mode do its work and hold the phone against a rail or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, once the lanterns are lit. For fewer people, go early in the morning, though the lanterns will not be glowing then.

text.access_note: This is a working Shinto shrine. Check the official site before you go.

name: Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
label: Ginkaku-ji
camera_source: Commons cluster (23 photos). Moved 82 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/105817561: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ginkaku-ji temple' (285 m across).

text.description: Ginkaku-ji, the Temple of the Silver Pavilion, is a Zen temple whose official name is Jishō-ji. It began as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, with plans dating from 1460, and became a temple after his death in 1490. The main building is the two-storey Kannon-den, started in 1482. Despite its nickname it was never covered in silver foil, and its plain, unfinished look is linked to the idea of wabi-sabi. That quiet look is why it photographs well. You get a simple wooden pavilion, a pond, mossy wooded grounds and a well-known sand garden, which includes a carefully formed sand mound said to stand for Mount Fuji. The buildings and ponds were planned around their surroundings, so the views were designed with care. Look for the pavilion with its pond reflection, the moss under the trees, and the sand garden with its mound. Take a few wide scene-setting shots first, then move in on details such as roof lines, moss and sand textures. Keep your phone steady against a rail or your own elbows when light is dim under the trees.
text.geographic_location: Ginkaku-ji is in Kyoto's Sakyo ward, at the foot of the Higashiyama hills on the eastern side of the city.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or transport app for the best way to reach Sakyo ward. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pavilion and pond. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the mossy garden and the sand garden, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and sand textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (south end of the pond). The Silver Pavilion (Kannon Hall) across the pond, framed by greenery and reflected in still water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pavilion on one third of the frame, leaving the pond in the rest to catch the reflection. For the sand garden, crouch low and, if any lines are visible in the sand, use them to lead the eye towards the sand mound. Keep the phone level so the horizontal lines of the building stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the pavilion, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and the pond reflection keep their detail. Wipe the lens first, and turn on Live Photos if you want a few moving ripples on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light, such as early in the day or on a lightly overcast day, suits the moss and the pavilion. Rain or damp weather can make the moss look richer, but protect your phone.

text.access_note: The garden and temple complex are open to the public; check the official site before you go for opening times and entry details.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft, even light, such as early in the day or on a lightly overcast day, generally suits photos of moss and wooden buildings.
Moss tends to look richer in colour when damp.
The pond may show reflections of the pavilion on calm days.
Entry to the grounds is likely to be through a ticketed gate and may have set hours.
Lines may be visible in the sand garden, but check on the day whether it is raked.

name: Gion and Hanamikoji Street
label: Gion
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9541222: large area 'Gion' (1509 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Gion is Kyoto's best-known geisha district, and Hanamikoji Street is its best-known traditional street. The street runs south from Shijō Street, where it is anchored by the famous Ichiriki Tei teahouse, down to the temple of Kennin-ji. Traditional machiya townhouses, some of them teahouses (ochaya), line the way. Some of them are ochaya, where geisha entertain guests at parties. The look is unusually tidy for a busy tourist area. Part of the district is a national historical preservation district, and since 1986 the city has removed electric poles from Hanamikoji and a few other popular streets. That keeps the sky and the rooflines clear of cables, which helps your photos.

The area is split into two geisha districts, Gion Kobu and the smaller Gion Higashi, which separated in 1881. Gion Kobu is the larger and includes Hanamikoji. Behind the street's calm look, Gion is also a lively tourist and nightlife area, so expect people in the frame.

For a phone photo, stand on the street and shoot along it, using the lines of the house fronts to lead the eye. Keep the phone level with gridlines on, and wait for a gap in the crowd. Do not step in front of anyone to get a shot. The houses are private, so stay on the street.
text.geographic_location: In Gion, part of Higashiyama-ku in eastern Kyoto, in front of Yasaka Shrine. Hanamikoji Street runs south from Shijō Street towards Kennin-ji.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Gion area at Shijō Street and find Hanamikoji Street, which runs south from there. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to squeeze the lanterns and house fronts together, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only in the tightest spots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there you look up the lane, with the machiya fronts on both sides leading towards the heart of the district.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame so the rooflines run level. Keep the phone upright for a tall, narrow street view. Include a little of the house fronts at the edges rather than cropping them out. If you want a different view, the Shirakawa River stretch in Gion, whose north bank is a pedestrian street lined with cherry trees, is a good second photo stop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the street to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so lit windows and lanterns do not wash out. After dark, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest time for a clear view. Around dusk, when the lights come on, the street looks warmer, though it is usually busier.

text.access_note: Hanamikoji is an open public street in a working district, but the houses along it are private, so stay on the street and check the official Kyoto tourism site before you go for any local photography rules.

name: Philosopher's Path
label: Philosopher's Path
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18344117: large area 'Philosopher's Walk' (1400 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Philosopher's Walk is a pedestrian path that follows a canal lined with cherry trees, running between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji in eastern Kyoto. It began as a path in 1890 and was extended in 1912, and it follows a shallow irrigation channel that carries water from the Lake Biwa Canal. The name comes from two Kyoto University professors and philosophers, Nishida Kitaro and Hajime Tanabe, who are thought to have walked it for daily exercise.

It photographs well because the scene is simple: still water, a narrow path and trees leaning over both. The line of the canal leads the eye along the frame, so even a quick snap looks composed. The whole walk takes about 30 minutes, though many people stop to visit the temples and shrines on the way, including Hōnen-in, Ōtoyo Shrine and Eikan-dō Zenrin-ji. On the northern part there are good views of the nearby Daimonji hill, which is a handy background if you turn away from the canal.

For photos, keep the canal edge on one side of the frame and let the path run diagonally into the distance. Add a person walking in the middle distance to give a sense of scale. The path is popular with tourists and locals, especially at cherry blossom time, so expect other walkers in your shots. Wait a moment for a gap, or use people as part of the scene.
text.geographic_location: In Kyoto, along a canal between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From there it is about 4 minutes on foot to the subject, heading south-east on the map and following the path beside the canal where it runs that way. The whole path is about 30 minutes' walk end to end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural views along the canal. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when the trees arch overhead, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a stretch of blossom or the Daimonji hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Suirokaku (rear of the Nanzen-ji grounds, on the canal side of the red-brick arches). shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the canal on a lower third line so the path leads into the frame. Hold the phone at chest height for a low, flowing view along the water, or lift it slightly to include more branches. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or let a single walker stand in as a scale figure.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky or blossom to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the petals and sky keep their detail. A Live Photo can catch falling blossom or a ripple on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Cherry blossom (hanami) season is the busiest and the most colourful. Whatever the season, going early in the day is likely to give you a quieter path.

text.description:
Ryōan-ji is a Zen temple in north-west Kyoto, and its dry rock garden is considered one of the finest surviving examples of a kare-sansui (dry landscape) garden. It is a plain rectangle of raked white gravel, about 25 metres by 10 metres, with fifteen stones set in five groups. Moss around the stones is the only plant life. The monks rake the gravel every day, so the lines are usually crisp. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto UNESCO World Heritage listing.

It photographs well because everything is so simple. You have pale gravel, dark stones and an old clay wall behind, stained brown and orange by age. The garden is meant to be viewed from the veranda of the abbot's hall, and the stones are arranged so that you can never see all fifteen at once. Nobody is certain who made the garden or exactly when. The version we see today dates from a rebuild at the end of the 1700s.

For your phone, think calm and uncluttered. Frame the whole rectangle first, then move in on one or two stone groups. The veranda can be busy, so be patient and take your shot when a gap opens. Rules about photography and where you may stand can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Ryōan-ji is in north-west Kyoto, and the rock garden lies in front of the main hall (hōjō) within the temple grounds.
text.directions_text: Once you are there, the garden is about 33 m to the north-west, which is about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole garden and the wall behind it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the stone groups and the moss. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close, and keep the garden's edges away from the corners of the frame, where lines can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. The garden is designed to be seen from the veranda of the hall, so use the viewing area facing the gravel and keep low and steady, as if you were sitting.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the top of the clay wall up with a horizontal line, so the gravel fills the lower part of the frame. Leave the wall in as a backdrop. Then try a tighter frame on one group of stones with the raked lines leading towards it. Remember that you will not be able to fit all fifteen stones into one view from the veranda.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: White gravel can fool the phone into making the picture too bright or too dark. Tap on the gravel to focus, then slide the exposure control down a little until the raked lines show clearly. Portrait mode and night mode are not needed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the temple opens, if you can, as the veranda tends to be quieter and you can take your time. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day also suits the gravel.

text.access_note: This is a Zen temple, so check the official site before you go for access and photography rules.

name: To-ji pagoda
label: To-ji
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak. Moved 146 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 45 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description: Tō-ji's five-storey pagoda is the tallest wooden tower in Japan, at 54.8 metres (180 feet). It is the landmark of the temple, which sits in Kyoto's Minami-ku ward. The temple was founded in 796, soon after the capital moved to Heian-kyō, and it is the only one of the three Buddhist temples first allowed in the city that still survives. The pagoda you see now dates from 1643, when the third Tokugawa shōgun, Iemitsu, ordered its rebuilding. Earlier versions were destroyed several times. It became a National Treasure in 1952, and the temple is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto. The pagoda photographs well because it is so tall and its outline is so clear. The tiers of eaves step neatly upwards, and the whole shape looks good against open sky. On a phone the main challenge is height. Stepping back and keeping the phone upright helps you fit more in, and zooming in lets you pick out the layered roofs. Include a bit of the temple grounds, trees or water in the foreground to give a sense of scale. The pagoda is normally closed to visitors, though you can usually see inside from outside. On the 21st of each month the grounds hold a well-known flea market, which is lively and good for atmosphere but busier, so plan your framing around people.
text.geographic_location: In Kyoto's Minami-ku ward, near the junction of Ōmiya Street and Kujō Street, south-west of Kyōto Station. The temple stands close to where the old Rashōmon gate once marked the southern edge of the Heian capital.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from Kyōto Station and head south-west towards the junction of Ōmiya Street and Kujō Street, where Tō-ji stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the whole pagoda. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stacked roofs, or use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want to include the grounds in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hyotan Pond (west of the five-story pagoda, inside the temple grounds). The pagoda rising above the pond and its surrounding trees, with a mirror reflection on calm mornings or evenings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central axis of the pagoda with a vertical grid line, keeping the phone upright rather than tilted back so the sides stay straight. Leave a little sky above the top spire, and include a tree, wall or pond edge at the bottom for depth. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky does not wash out and the wood and tiles keep their detail. If you use a Live Photo, hold still for a moment before and after the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Expect more visitors on the 21st of each month, when the flea market is held.

text.access_note: Tō-ji is a Buddhist temple and a World Heritage Site, and parts of it may be ticketed or have set visiting hours, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:

Turn on the gridlines and line up the pagoda with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower look as if it is falling backwards. Take a few portrait-format (upright) shots first, since the pagoda is taller than it is wide, then try one landscape frame that includes more of the surroundings.

text.description:
Daigo-ji is a very large Buddhist temple on the south-eastern edge of Kyoto, at the foot of Mount Daigo (Kasatoriyama). Its grounds cover over 6.6 million square metres, and it is one of the 17 parts of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto". This spot is in Shimo-Daigo, the lower part of the temple: one large enclosure with separate halls and open ground between them. The temple was founded in 874. Shimo-Daigo's Kondō was built in 926, and a five-storey pagoda followed in 951. When fire swept through during the Ōnin War, the pagoda was the only building left standing in Shimo-Daigo. Toyotomi Hideyoshi later held his famous cherry blossom viewing here.

It photographs well because of the space. The buildings stand apart, so you can frame a hall or roofline with trees and sky around it instead of squeezing it between other visitors. Because the enclosure is so large, walk round a little before choosing your shot. The nearby Sambō-in area has cherry-lined streets and is lively in blossom season, so expect people in your pictures then. Turn on the gridlines to keep the timber lines straight, and take a few frames at different distances. Some parts need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Daigo-ji is in Fushimi-ku, on the south-eastern side of Kyoto City, at the foot of Mount Daigo (Kasatoriyama). This spot is in Shimo-Daigo, the lower part of the temple grounds.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or the official site for how to reach the lower temple grounds (Shimo-Daigo). Check the official site before you go for entry arrangements for the different parts of the temple. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a hall or the pagoda with some space around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open ground and trees, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof edges and carved timber.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Move a few steps either way until no passers-by block the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the building on a third line, with trees or sky filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the tall timber lines stay straight. Take one wide frame for the setting and one closer frame for detail. Cherry-lined streets near Sambō-in are a good extra subject in blossom season.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. If the scene is dull, try a Live Photo so you can pick a moment with fewer people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring, when the cherry blossom is out, is a lively time at Sambō-in, so expect more people. Arriving early in the day is a sensible way to get cleaner shots.

name: Pontocho and the Kamo River
label: Pontocho
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

text.description:
Pontocho is a long, narrow alleyway in Kyoto, running between Shijō-dōri and Sanjō-dōri one block west of the Kamo River. It is a hanamachi, a traditional geisha district, and is known for its geiko and maiko, its tea houses and its preserved old architecture. The district's crest is a stylised water plover, or chidori. The name is thought to come from the Portuguese word for bridge, "ponte".

It photographs well because the scene is layered. There are wooden façades, rows of lanterns and, along the river side, restaurants with outdoor wooden dining patios. At night the traditional lanterns light the whole area, which gives a warm glow that suits a phone camera. The Kamo River beside it gives you open space and a long view, which is a nice contrast with the tight alley.

At the Sanjō-dōri end stands the Ponto-chō Kaburenjō Theatre. It is a practice hall for geisha and maiko, and it has hosted the annual Kamogawa Odori dance performance since the 1870s.

For your photos, try one wide view along the river and one closer shot of lanterns and wooden fronts. Keep the lanterns as your bright points and let the rest fall into soft shadow. If you see a geiko or maiko, be polite and keep your distance.
text.geographic_location: Pontocho is in Kyoto, in the narrow strip between Shijō-dōri and Sanjō-dōri, one block west of the Kamo River. On the opposite bank of the river stands a statue of Izumo no Okuni, the founder of kabuki.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 460 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the river and the general scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the narrow alley, where it helps you fit in the lanterns and the rooflines. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out lanterns, signs or the riverside patios from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 460 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Then walk north to the alley for the close-up shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals of the buildings straight. Try to include a line of lanterns leading into the frame. From the riverside, use the telephoto lens to compress the patios and lanterns into one tidy picture. Keep a respectful distance from any geiko or maiko, and do not block the alley.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: In the evening, tap on a lantern to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour. Use night mode in the dark alley and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing. Live Photos can also catch the movement of passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and early evening, when the lanterns are lit and there is still some blue in the sky.

text.access_note: The alley is a public street, but the restaurants, tea houses and theatre are private businesses, so check local signs before you go.

text.description: Kyoto Tower is a slim white observation tower right opposite Kyōto Station, and it is the tallest structure in the city. The observation deck is at 100 metres and the spire reaches 131 metres. It was designed to look something like a Japanese candle, and it was built in 1964 on the site of the former central post office. Instead of an open metal lattice, it uses stacked steel rings covered in welded steel sheets. It stands on a nine-storey building with a hotel and shops. Kyoto's height limits keep most of the neighbouring buildings low, so the tower stands out against the sky. That makes it easy to photograph as a clean, simple shape. The tower has always divided opinion because it looks so modern in an old capital, and that contrast is part of the picture: a smooth white spire above ordinary city streets and the station's glass-and-steel frontage. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south of the subject. At this distance the whole tower will not fit in the default lens (1x) held upright, so use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and tilt up. Keep the phone level to stop the tower leaning. Include a little of the street or the building at its base to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Kyoto Tower is in central Kyoto, directly opposite Kyōto Station.
text.directions_text: Kyoto Tower stands directly across the street from Kyōto Station, so the station is the easiest place to start. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower and some foreground into one upright frame. Use the default lens (1x) only if you want a tighter shot of the upper part of the tower. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for close shots of the spire or the observation deck against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Look for a spot where the street or building edges lead up towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and use the ultra-wide (0.5x). Put the tower slightly off-centre and keep some of the street or the base building in the frame. Switch on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the spire to keep it straight. Wires and signs can creep in at this distance, so move a few steps sideways if they spoil the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white tower keeps its detail against a bright sky. Use night mode after dark, and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sky is usually clearer and the light softer. If the tower is lit after dark, dusk is a good time for a night-mode shot.

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a city street, but the observation deck is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Heian Shrine is a Shinto shrine in Kyoto's Okazaki area, and it is one of the most photogenic places on the map because of its bright red buildings and very large gate. It was built for the 1895 exhibition marking 1,100 years since Kyoto (then Heian-kyō) was founded. It is a partial copy of the old Heian Palace at 5/8 of the original size, designed by Itō Chūta. The big red entrance gate copies the palace's Outenmon, and the shrine's torii is one of the largest in Japan. The shrine also has a Japanese-style garden covering about half the grounds, with ponds fed by water from the Lake Biwa Canal. Part of the shrine burned down in 1976, including the main sanctuary, and it was rebuilt three years later with donations. The strong red against sky, white gravel and green trees gives you a clear, simple picture even on a basic phone. Stand back far enough to fit the whole gate in, then move closer for roof corners, painted beams and gravel patterns. Keep people in the frame for a sense of scale, but wait a moment for a gap if the courtyard is busy. If you visit on 22 October, the Jidai Matsuri festival procession ends at the shrine, which gives you extra colour for photos.
text.geographic_location: Heian Shrine is in the Okazaki area of Sakyō-ku, Kyoto. It sits beside Okazaki Park, with the Kyoto Municipal Museum of Art and the National Museum of Modern Art nearby.
text.directions_text: Head for the Okazaki area of Sakyō-ku, around Okazaki Park, by taxi or hired scooter. Walk north-east towards the middle of the shrine area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and courtyard as you see them. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole gate and sky in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details, carvings and the red-and-white colour contrast.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jingū-michi (south side, looking north toward the great torii). The roughly 24 m torii framed along the approach avenue, with the vermilion gate at the far end for scale. From here you look towards the middle of the shrine area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gate on one of the vertical lines so the roofline sits level. Hold the phone steady and keep it upright so the pillars don't lean. Leave some gravel in the foreground to lead the eye in. For a closer picture, use telephoto on one roof corner against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. This keeps the red rich and the white walls from glaring. If you are shooting people in front of the gate, try portrait mode only when they are a few steps from the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Overcast days also suit the strong red colour.

text.access_note: Parts of the shrine, especially the garden, may be ticketed or have set opening times, so check the official site before you go. Please be respectful as this is a working place of worship.

text.description: Tōfuku-ji is a large Zen temple in Kyoto's Higashiyama-ku, founded in 1236 by the imperial chancellor Kujō Michiie. It is one of the Kyoto Gozan, the "five great Zen temples" of the city. Its main gate is the oldest sanmon in Japan and a National Treasure, and the complex has 24 sub-temples today. For photographers, though, the draw is the maple-filled Sengyokukan ravine. The temple has a great many Japanese maples, and looking at the autumn leaves from the Tsūten-kyō bridge is a long-standing tradition. The best-known picture is taken from the covered bridge Gaunkyo (臥雲橋). From there you look back up the ravine and see the covered Tsutenkyo walkway framed by the trees. The view works because the walkway gives the scene a clear focal point, and the trees fill the rest of the frame with colour. The temple is busiest in the autumn leaf season, so expect crowds then. In the peak weeks, some parts may have ticketed entry, and photography on the bridges may be limited, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone ready, work quickly in busy spells, and don't block the path while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Tōfuku-ji is in Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, with the Sengyokukan ravine and its covered bridges on the approach path. Sennyū-ji, another large temple, is nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best route to Tōfuku-ji in Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, then follow the approach path towards the ravine and the covered bridge Gaunkyo (臥雲橋). Allow extra time in the autumn leaf season, when the paths are busy. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole ravine with the walkway framed by maples. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the covered Tsutenkyo walkway and its trees. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people crowd the bridge and you want a broader scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 臥雲橋 (Covered bridge on the approach path, a little downstream of Tsutenkyo). Looking back up the Sengyokukan ravine, the covered Tsutenkyo walkway is framed against the maple-filled valley. From here you look back up the Sengyokukan ravine and see the covered Tsutenkyo walkway set against the maple-filled valley. The temple lies to the south-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the walkway up with a horizontal grid line so it sits level. Let the maples fill the foreground and the sides of the frame. Guides describe this as the classic postcard angle. If you want a different view, Tsutenkyo itself gives a sweeping look down over the red maples, with temple roofs among the trees. Selfie sticks and tripods are reportedly banned on the bridge, so hold your phone with both hands and keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest leaves to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the reds stay rich and don't wash out. Take a few shots in a row, because people move through the frame quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when guides say the light is soft and the crowds are thinner. The peak autumn season runs from mid-November to early December and is the busiest.

text.access_note: The temple grounds are a working Zen temple. The peak autumn season brings ticketed entry to Tsutenkyo and Kaizando, and photography on the bridges may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Higashi Hongan-ji is the head temple of the Ōtani-ha branch of Jōdo Shinshū in Kyoto, and locals know it affectionately as Ohigashisan, 'Honorable Mr. East'. It photographs well because of its sheer scale. The main hall, the Goei-dō, is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world, at 76 metres long, 58 metres wide and 38 metres high. It holds an image of the founder, Shinran. The hall you see today dates from 1895, after a long run of fires; the Amida Hall beside it was rebuilt in the same year. The temple itself was founded in 1602 by the shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu, and the Shinran mausoleum has stood on its current site since 1670. All of this gives you dark timber, deep roofs and big open courtyards to work with. The hall is so large that the main challenge is fitting it in. Stepping back and using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) lets you include the full roofline and some sky, while the default lens (1x) suits a calmer, more balanced view of the front. If you want details such as roof ends, carved timber or lanterns, use the telephoto lens instead. Keep other visitors small in the frame, as they help show how big the building is. This is a working temple, so keep your voice and your phone low during services and follow any signs about where photography is not allowed.
text.geographic_location: Higashi Hongan-ji lies in central Kyoto, in a large temple precinct. It is a large complex with several halls inside one set of grounds.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so from central Kyoto the simplest way is by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Higashi Hongan-ji. That is about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the full width of the Goei-dō, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, carved details and lanterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roof ridge with a horizontal line so the huge hall does not look tilted. Keep your phone level and stand back far enough to avoid the roof leaning inwards. Include a few people or an open stretch of courtyard in the foreground to show how big the building is. Try a second shot with the nearby Amida Hall to the left of the Goei-dō.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wooden walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the dark timber keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as moving visitors will change the scene each time.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the timber and fewer people in the courtyard. Avoid the middle of the day if you want to reduce harsh shadows under the roofs.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any rules about photography inside the halls.

text.description:
Shinsen-en is a garden in Kyoto, ranked 20 on this map. Gardens like this photograph well on a phone because water, trees and old-style buildings tend to sit together in one frame. That gives you layers and reflections without needing anything fancy.

Use it as your starting place, then head west towards the garden, about 249 m away (roughly 3–4 minutes on foot). I can't give you history, size or dates for the garden here, so read the notices on site or the official website for the background.

For photos, start wide and then go close. Take one overall picture to show the setting, then look for smaller scenes: a branch over the water, a stone lantern, a roof edge framed by leaves. Keep the horizon level using gridlines. If the garden has a pond, tap on the brightest part of the scene and then pull the exposure slider down a touch, so the sky doesn't wash out and the water keeps its colour. Move slowly, stay in public areas and be mindful of other visitors. Check the official site before you go, as access rules for a garden like this can change.
text.geographic_location: Shinsen-en garden is in Kyoto, on the Kyoto map, where it is ranked 20.
text.directions_text: From there the garden is about 249 m to the west, roughly 3–4 minutes on foot. Follow the compass direction west and check the map as you go. The phone icon on the map is about 210 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the general view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the space is narrow and you can't step back. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as lanterns, leaves and reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 210 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Check on site what you can photograph from public areas.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the water's edge or a roofline with a horizontal line. Use a branch or a gateway in the foreground to frame the scene. Take one wide shot, then move closer for two or three detail shots. Portrait mode works well for a single leaf, lantern or flower against a soft background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your main subject, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright. If you want a sense of movement, such as ripples or wind in the leaves, try Live Photos. Keep your phone steady against your body, or rest it on something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday sun can make strong contrasts under the trees, so check the scene before you shoot.

text.access_note: Access and any entry rules are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.
